description: A peer server-fn (`lookupOne`, escalated by its own `?{}`) is called inside a synchronous `.sort` comparator within another server function. Per §13.2 the compiler cannot insert `await` in a sync callback, so the bare emission would return an always-truthy Promise into the comparator. E-SERVER-FN-IN-SYNC-CALLBACK fires (§34: Error), fail-closed. This code was LIVE but UNCATALOGUED until S305 added its §34 row — the sibling E-ASYNC-STDLIB-IN-SYNC-CALLBACK named it in prose while it had no row of its own, so the freeze gate could neither pin nor honestly defer it. NOTE: both halves also emit `E-PA-002` (protect-analyzer). That is a CONSTANT of the borrowed `<db src= protect= tables=>` fixture shape — the already-landed sibling case `auth/auth-async-stdlib-sync-callback-neg` emits it too — so it is inherited, not introduced here, and the codes-half superset check leaves this case precise about its own target. Worth a look on its own terms though: E-PA-002 reads "invalid `protect=` syntax" against a `protect="password_hash"` that looks well-formed.
rationale: §13.2 — scrml has no source `await` (§13.1), so the compiler auto-awaits a peer server-fn call wherever an `await` can be inserted. A synchronous callback body is exactly where it cannot: the callback must RETURN a value to its caller (`.sort` needs a number, `.some` a boolean), and a Promise is always truthy — so a bare emission would make every comparison succeed. The failure is silent and data-dependent, which is why §49 makes it FAIL-CLOSED at compile time rather than a runtime surprise. The `for`-loop form is the sanctioned restructuring: the loop body IS the server function's async body, so the await goes in.
